title: A slice decomposition with A(x): how is the solid built up?
summary: A solid of revolution is cut into thin disks across its axis. The left panel shows the slices, one of them highlighted; the right panel plots the area A(x) of each slice, and the area under that curve is the volume.

media.alt: Left: a teal profile curve and its mirror image with 12 vertical strips, one highlighted in amber at x = 1.25, and a rose line for the axis of revolution. Right: a blue curve A(x) with the area to the left of the amber dashed line shaded teal, an amber dot on the curve and the label V = 4.48.
media.caption: Reference render of class F3.3 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data. Standard theory only.

read_the_figure.question: How is the solid built up?
read_the_figure.axes: Left: x along the axis (0 to 2) and radius r (-1.9 to 1.9), equal scale; the rose line is the axis of revolution. Right: x (0 to 2) against cross-section area A(x) = pi r(x)^2 in square units; the shaded area is the volume so far, and the amber dashed line and dot show the current slice.
look_at: Pick the amber slice: what is its radius at x = 1.25 and what is its area?
Where is A(x) largest and does it coincide with the largest radius?
What does the shaded area on the right measure?
Is the stepped sum of 12 slices close to the smooth integral?
as_drawn: The radius is r(x) = 0.6 + 0.8 sin(pi x/2)(1 - x/4); at x = 1.25, r = 1.108 and A = 3.86 (the dot on the right).
The volume so far to x = 1.25 is printed as 4.48; the exact integral is 4.49. The total volume is 6.29; the twelve disks sum to 6.30.
The left panel uses equal scale, so the solid looks thin; the right panel shows area in different units and a different vertical scale.
read_the_figure.proves: That the volume is the accumulated slice area and that the slices add up to it. It does not prove the profile is correct: that is an input.
if_wrong: The slice thickness not uniform: sum of areas times thickness is wrong.
A(x) drawn for a different slice orientation than the left picture: the two panels no longer match.
Radius plotted against area on one axis: units differ.

terms.meaning: A solid made by spinning a plane region about a line (the axis).
The shape of the solid cut by a plane perpendicular to the axis: a disk here.
The area of that disk, A = pi r^2.
Volume as the integral of slice areas along the axis.
Volume as the integral of thin cylindrical shells around the axis, used when the region is spun about a line parallel to the slicing direction.
The width of each slice along the axis.

remember: V = integral of A(x) dx, with A the area of a slice perpendicular to x.
Disk: A = pi r^2. Washer: A = pi (R^2 - r^2).
Colour the current slice; link it to the A(x) curve.
Units: A in length squared, V in length cubed.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Left: rectangles stand for disks seen edge-on; the amber one is the current slice and the rose line is the axis. Right: a line for the area curve, a filled region for accumulated volume, and a dot at the current slice. A dashed line in both panels ties them together.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: A volume is an accumulation of areas. The left picture shows what is being sliced; the right shows the single number per slice. By moving the amber slice you see that the dot slides along the A curve, and that the shaded area is the integral. The picture turns the formula V = integral of A dx into something you can follow with the eye.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: With equal axes the solid looks thin and the areas look small relative to the radii. Because A is r squared, a 20 percent change in radius is a 44 percent change in area: the right curve looks more dramatic than the left. Rectangles overshoot the curve where r is rising. And a few slices give a staircase that is not the smooth integral.

understand.title: Why each required item matters
understand.text: Highlighting the current slice lets the reader connect panels. Linking A(x) to the slice makes the volume an area under a curve. The scale and units on A make the left's radius and the right's area two different quantities.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: For the shape itself use a 3D cutaway (F3.5). For a region spun about a line parallel to the slices, shells are easier. For volume without calculus, Pappus' theorem uses the centroid. For a sphere or a cone, check the answer against the known closed form.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Animate the amber slice from x = 0 to 2 while the shaded area grows and the volume reading updates; add the shell decomposition of the same solid beside it.

steps.title: Volume as an integral of slice areas
steps.note: With r(x) = 0.6 + 0.8 sin(pi x/2)(1 - x/4): total V = 6.289; up to x = 1.25 the volume is 4.490 (the render's 4.48 comes from its sample grid). Twelve midpoint disks give 6.298, 0.13 percent high.

steps.title: A check against a known solid
steps.note: For a = 2, V = 32 pi / 3 = 33.51, which is what the numerical sum gives and what the Studio's sphere example shows.

worked.title: Reading the reference render
worked.problem: From the figure: (1) what is the radius and area of the amber slice at x = 1.25? (2) Where is A largest? (3) What is the volume up to x = 1.25?

solution.text: The right dot is at A of about 3.86, so r = sqrt(3.86 / pi) = 1.11, matching the amber strip's height on the left.
Near x = 0.87 (A = 4.6): the radius also peaks near there, since A = pi r^2.
The shaded area under A up to the dashed line: about 4.5.

worked.answer: Amber slice r = 1.11, A = 3.86; A peaks near x = 0.87; volume so far 4.49 out of 6.29.

analyze.q: Why does A(x) look more peaked than the radius profile?
If the solid were spun about the line y = 1 instead of y = 0, what would change in A(x)?
How would the figure change for shells? Which panel would need a different quantity?

evaluate.q: A CAD tool reports volume by summing 12 slices. How would you check its accuracy using this form of plot?
evaluate.hint: Compare with a finer sum and the midpoint-rule error.

create: Plot the cumulative volume V(x) as a third panel, with the final value labelled.
Draw the same solid with the shell decomposition and compare the two integrals.

checks.q: What does the area under the A(x) curve represent?
A slice has radius 2. What is its area, and what is the volume of a 0.1 thick slice?
Twelve disks give 6.298 and the exact volume is 6.289. Is a staircase approximation of a smooth solid likely to over- or under-estimate?
checks.hint: Midpoint rule and curvature of A.
checks.answer: The midpoint-rule error here is 0.13 percent high; the sign depends on the concavity of A(x). Check against a finer sum.
